intro: Becoming, in Layers explores the relationship between fashion and personal identity through clothing, textiles, photography and mixed media. Drawing from my cultural heritage, memories and personal experiences, I use fashion as a form of self-expression and visual storytelling. The exhibition reflects how different parts of our lives come together to shape who we are and who we are becoming.
bio: Koketso Masemola is a South African multidisciplinary emerging artist, creative and commercial model. She is currently studying Visual Multimedia Arts at the University of South Africa (UNISA) and screenwriting at Star Quality. She is also gaining practical experience in the film and television industry through her internship at Bomb Productions.

Her creative interests include painting, photography, fashion, filmmaking and visual storytelling. She particularly enjoys painting landscapes, exploring different artistic techniques and capturing images through photography.

Beyond visual arts, Masemola is a commercial model represented by Aurora Talent Agency and a social media content creator. Her love for dressing up and experimenting with different fashion styles has become an important part of how she expresses herself. She enjoys exploring different looks and using clothing to communicate different sides of her personality.

These interests influence her artistic practice, particularly her exploration of identity through fashion. Her exhibition, Becoming, in Layers (2026), reflects her interest in how clothing, cultural heritage, personal memories and creative expression contribute to a person's identity.
Through her work, Masemola continues to explore different ways of telling stories, expressing herself and connecting her interests in visual art, fashion and film.
statement: My artistic practice explores identity through fashion, focusing on how clothing can communicate personal experiences, cultural belonging and self-expression.

For this exhibition, I worked with garments, fabrics, photographs and mixed media to explore different aspects of who I am. I was interested in the idea that identity is not something fixed, but something that continues to develop as we grow and experience life.

The title Becoming, in Layers reflects this process. Just as clothing is made through the combination of different materials, I see my identity as being formed through different experiences, memories, interests and cultural influences.

My use of traditional-inspired fabrics connects to my cultural background, while personal photographs bring elements of memory and individual experience into the work. I also experimented with transparency, layering, stitching and contrasting materials to explore the relationship between what we show to others and what remains personal.

Rather than presenting one complete definition of myself, my artworks reflect an ongoing process of becoming. Through fashion and material experimentation, I invite viewers to consider the different layers that contribute to their own identities.
catalogue: As my project developed, I began experimenting with other ways of representing identity beyond the main garment. This led me to create a series of smaller mixed-media works using fabric, photographs, lace, crochet and other materials. Although these works were developed at a later stage, they allowed me to explore the idea of identity through different forms and surfaces.

In Fragments of Self, I combined personal photographs with different fabrics inside triangular frames. I was interested in how the materials interacted visually, particularly when transparent lace was placed over photographs. Looking at the completed pieces, I began to consider how the visible and partially covered images could suggest different aspects of identity. This connected to my broader idea that people are made up of experiences and influences that are not always immediately visible.

I also created Rooted in Change, a figure incorporating an Afro, traditional-inspired fabric and white organza. The contrast between the patterned fabric and the softer, transparent material allowed me to experiment with the appearance of traditional clothing. Although the white skirt could resemble bridal clothing, my intention was not to represent marriage. Instead, I used the material to explore a different visual interpretation of a culturally inspired garment.

My small crocheted dress, Threads of Home, approached the theme through the act of making. Inspired by Pedi clothing, the work brought cultural identity into a handmade form. The repeated loops of crochet also connected to my interest in the different elements that contribute to a person's identity.

In Held Together, I moved away from the recognizable shape of clothing while continuing to work with textile materials. I combined brick-like forms made from different fabrics with a stretched stocking, holes and pins. The relationship between these materials created a contrast between construction and vulnerability. Reflecting on the work, I began to see a connection to the way identity is built from different influences and can change over time.

Together, these works expanded my exploration of identity through fashion. They allowed me to consider clothing and textiles not only as things we wear, but also as materials through which ideas about memory, belonging, visibility and personal development can be explored.
works: Becoming, in Layers
Mixed media installation incorporating a garment, textiles and photographic imagery.
Medium to be confirmed against the finished piece.

Becoming, in Layers explores identity as something that is continuously shaped by personal experiences, cultural influences and self-expression. The garment becomes a way of representing the self, while the different materials suggest the many aspects that contribute to identity.
Fragments of Self
Mixed media: framed triangular forms, textiles, lace and photographic prints.

Fragments of Self consists of triangular compositions combining fabric and personal photographs. The different materials create separate visual sections, suggesting that identity is made up of many parts rather than one complete image.

In some sections, photographs are partially covered by transparent lace. This creates a relationship between visibility and concealment, suggesting that some aspects of ourselves are easily seen while others remain beneath the surface.
The work explores how different fragments of personal experience can exist together to form a developing sense of self.
Rooted in Change
Mixed media textile artwork incorporating fabric, traditional-inspired textiles and organza.
Rooted in Change explores the relationship between cultural identity and personal expression through a female figure dressed in a combination of fabrics.

The Afro and traditional-inspired clothing connect the figure to cultural heritage, while the contrasting materials introduce a more contemporary interpretation of dress. The white organza adds lightness and transparency, contrasting with the patterned fabric and strips extending from the hips.

Rather than representing bridal clothing, the white fabric is used as a visual layer that changes the shape and appearance of the garment. The artwork considers how cultural identity can remain meaningful while allowing space for change, experimentation and individual expression.
Threads of Home
Crocheted textile artwork.
Threads of Home is a small crocheted dress inspired by Pedi traditional clothing. Through the handmade garment, I explore the relationship between cultural belonging, fashion and personal identity.

The process of building the dress through repeated loops connects to the wider exhibition's interest in how separate elements come together to form something whole. Its small scale also encourages closer attention to the details of the garment.
The artwork presents cultural identity through a personal interpretation of clothing and the act of making.
Held Together
Mixed media: assorted textiles, nylon stocking and pins.
Support material to be confirmed.

Held Together combines brick-like forms made from different materials beneath a stretched stocking. The repeated shapes suggest construction, while the stocking creates a surface that both covers and exposes what lies underneath.

The holes and pins interrupt this surface, creating a sense of tension and vulnerability. These material relationships can be understood as a metaphor for identity: something built from different influences, held together through experience and continually affected by change.
The artwork extends the exhibition's exploration of identity beyond clothing itself, using textile materials to investigate the relationship between structure, protection and exposure.
